bio.en: Ebi Atawodi is the director of product management at YouTube, where she oversees the creator experience, and previously led payments and fintech product at Uber and Netflix.
bio.zh: Ebi Atawodi 是 YouTube 的产品管理总监，负责创作者体验，此前曾在 Uber 和 Netflix 主导支付与金融科技产品。

summary.en: Ebi shares some of the most tactical advice Lenny has heard on developing a clear product vision and communicating it effectively to both teammates and executives. She breaks down the craft of product management and how to deliberately get better at it, plus what she's learned about building a strong product culture within a team and across a company. Her philosophy centers on leading with care—'being loved, not liked'—so that hard feedback lands in service of people's growth.
summary.zh: Ebi 分享了 Lenny 听过最具实操性的一些建议，内容是如何打造清晰的产品愿景，并有效地向同事和高管沟通。她拆解了产品管理的“手艺”以及如何有意识地精进，还谈到了在团队和公司层面建立强产品文化的心得。她的理念核心是以关怀来领导——追求“被爱，而非被喜欢”，让尖锐的反馈真正服务于人的成长。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: I do not believe in being liked. I believe in being loved, right? And that's a very, very different thing. When I said this once in a meeting, people were like... Yes, right? But it took me a while in reading a lot of books to come to a definition of love and love is the choice to extend yourself for the spiritual growth of oneself or another, right? It's very big, lofty and whatever, but you're literally extending yourself for somebody else or yourself, self-love, right? And that's love. And when you are extending yourself, you're not nice. It's not always nice or like, it sometimes is having hard conversations. It's knowing that, oh, there's a human, they know I care about them. So when the feedback is coming like raw, they know that it's in their best interest because I've shown enough times that I genuinely care about the person behind the role.
turns.zh: 我不相信被人喜欢。我相信被爱，对吗？这是非常非常不同的事情。当我在一次会议上说过这句话时，人们就像……是的，对吗？但我花了一段时间阅读了很多书籍才得出爱的定义，爱是为了自己或他人的精神成长而扩展自己的选择，对吧？它非常大、崇高等等，但你实际上是在为别人或你自己延伸自己，自爱，对吧？这就是爱。当你扩展自己时，你就不好了。并不总是友好或喜欢，有时会进行艰难的对话。它知道，哦，有一个人，他们知道我关心他们。因此，当收到原始反馈时，他们知道这符合他们的最大利益，因为我已经多次表明我真正关心这个角色背后的人。

turns.en: It's my pleasure. And so here we are. I want to start by talking about vision. Every product manager I've ever worked with and managed vision has always been this development area for every single one. It's always this like, "You need to get better at crafting a vision, telling your story." It's also this very powerful tool. The product managers have to align teams to be more successful in the products they're building. And you have a really neat way of thinking about a framework for developing a vision and then telling the story. What are elements of a good vision for a product or even a company?
turns.zh: 这是我的荣幸。首先，我想向 Andre Albuquerque 表示衷心的感谢，他是 One Month PM 的创始人，他在 LinkedIn 上发帖表示他是你的粉丝，我需要你加入这个播客。我们就到这里了。我想首先谈谈愿景。与我共事过并管理愿景的每一位产品经理始终是每个人的发展领域。总是这样的，“你需要更好地制定愿景，讲述你的故事。”这也是一个非常强大的工具。产品经理必须协调团队，以便在他们正在构建的产品中取得更大的成功。你有一种非常巧妙的方式来思考一个框架来制定愿景，然后讲述故事。产品甚至公司的良好愿景的要素是什么？

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: I think the first piece is that you absolutely need to have one, to start by saying that. Regardless of what level you are in the company. So people say, "Oh, I'm just a junior PM." Whatever level, there is some micro macro vision that you need to have. Because essentially if you got on a plane and the pilot was like, "I don't really know where we're going, but I'm a really good pilot. The company needs to fly 400 flights this year. So I'm trying to make that happen, but trust me, we'll get there. There might be turbulence, I'm not sure." You probably would be thinking twice about staying on that flight, right? What happens is you get on there, it's like, "Our destination is Miami." Maybe I'm dreaming of beaches, "And it's going to be 24 degrees when we get there." And he always paints or she paints this image of the destination. (00:06:13): And that's the vision not to be confused with the mission, which is we want to fly people where they're going safe. That's not... It's like a picture. So that's the start. I want to just delineate between vision and everything else that people think vision is. So really I think there are a couple of key elements. The first one is it needs to be lofty. So it needs to be something that feels... It almost scares you in an exciting way, right? Like, oh, my God, this is something I can get up every morning. And if we did that, goddamn. But at the same time, it needs to be realistic and attainable, so it cannot feel so pie in the sky that it feels so out of reach, right? And of course, there are leaders and people who have really, really big visions and they see beyond the rest of us, but that's not most people. Most people, it needs to feel within reach. (00:07:05): And then I think the key thing is it needs to kind of be in a vacuum from the limitations of today because the whole point of going to the future and saying, [inaudible 00:07:15] time traveled five years out is to say, "Okay, I've come back to tell you what we need to fix in order to get there. Or I've come back to tell you what we need to put in place now so that we will get there, right?" And so you have this kind of three components and if those come together and they are grounded of course, in a problem that people are excited about, you've got your vision. And how that vision manifests really depends on what you want to do. There're simple ones you can do, they're big ones you can do. But those are the core pieces in my mind.
turns.zh: 我认为第一件事是你绝对需要有一个，首先要说的是。不管你在公司处于什么级别。所以人们会说：“哦，我只是一名初级总理。”无论级别如何，您都需要具备一些微观宏观视野。因为基本上，如果你登上飞机，飞行员会说，“我真的不知道我们要去哪里，但我是一名非常优秀的飞行员。公司今年需要飞行 400 次航班。所以我正在努力实现这一目标，但相信我，我们会到达那里。可能会有湍流，我不确定。”您可能会再三考虑是否要继续乘坐该航班，对吧？发生的事情是，当你到达那里时，就像“我们的目的地是迈阿密”。也许我梦想着海滩，“当我们到达那里时，气温将是 24 度。”他或她总是画出目的地的形象。 (00:06:13)：不要将这一愿景与我们的使命相混淆，即我们希望将人们带到安全的地方。那不是……这就像一幅画。这就是开始。我想简单地界定一下愿景和人们所认为的愿景的其他一切。所以我真的认为有几个关键要素。第一个是它需要崇高。所以它需要让人感觉……它几乎以一种令人兴奋的方式吓到你，对吧？就像，天哪，这是我每天早上都能起床的事情。如果我们这么做了，该死的。但同时，它又必须是现实的、可实现的，所以不能感觉天上掉馅饼，遥不可及，对吧？当然，有些领导者和人们有着非常非常远大的愿景，他们的眼光超越了我们其他人，但大多数人并不是这样。对于大多数人来说，它需要感觉触手可及。 (00:07:05)：然后我认为关键是它需要摆脱今天的限制，因为走向未来并说，[听不清 00:07:15] 五年后的时间就是说，“好吧，我回来告诉你我们需要解决什么才能到达那里。或者我回来告诉你我们现在需要采取什么措施才能到达那里，对吗？”所以你有这样的三个组成部分，如果它们结合在一起并且它们当然扎根于人们感兴趣的问题，你就得到了你的愿景。这个愿景如何体现实际上取决于你想做什么。您可以做一些简单的事情，也可以做一些大的事情。但这些是我心中的核心部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you just summarize them again and are some examples you can share if here's a really good vision that it hits on these, and then if you have another example of a bad vision, that would be really helpful?
turns.zh: 您能否再次总结一下它们，并举一些可以分享的例子，如果这是一个非常好的愿景，那么如果您有另一个坏愿景的例子，那会很有帮助吗？

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: So four things. So it has to be lofty, it has to be realistic, it has to be devoid of any tech or limitations of today, and it has to be grounded in a very clear and potent problem. User problem.
turns.zh: 所以有四件事。所以它必须是崇高的，它必须是现实的，它必须没有任何技术或当今的限制，它必须基于一个非常明确和有效的问题。用户问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And then, yeah, are there any examples either from places you've worked or visions?
turns.zh: 惊人的。然后，是的，有没有来自你工作过的地方或愿景的例子？

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Absolutely. What I particularly love, so a lot of my product thinking and my product chops and craft, I really owe to Uber. So when I think about things, there's something really magical there. And one of our values at the time was making magic. So I met the word magic all the time, but so mission, push a button, get a ride, transportation as reliable as running water. I used to be in Nigeria, that tagline did not scale because water was not that reliable in Nigeria. So they went for a slightly more inclusive version, which is reliable transport, sanitation everywhere and for everyone, right? So that's the mission. That doesn't really tell me what the image looks like when I get there, but that's like when I wake up every day, I'm like, "Why do I work in this company?" It's that make transportation reliable everywhere for everyone. (00:09:12): And I'll talk maybe later about how that came to... We were able to use that to actually challenge the then CEO Travis Kalanick. The vision was a world where you get to this continuous trip so that you do not need parking. Because cities, 25% of the average city is parking spaces. You're in San Francisco, you'll see buildings, just floors just for parking, right? You'll have basements just for parking. In a world where we have housing problems, we have ridiculous prices for rents. Just imagine if you could free up all of those spaces for all kinds of things, right? Homes, restaurants, you name it. Parties, warehouse parties especially, they have the best. That was the vision. You could kind of see it, right? You're like, "Oh, I could see a world." I mean, I live in Amsterdam, I have a bicycle, I can see it every other day. They're getting rid of cars and actually converting the parking lots on the street into communal gardens, right? (00:10:16): So it's not crazy. It's attainable. But now doing that for the whole world, what does that look like? And that's how things like Uber Pool came in where in a world where the average car has 1.5 people in it, we can maximize that and then we can get this connected trip where the car is just moving and then maybe the car is autonomous, so you don't actually have to drive that car, and so it just doesn't need to stop. I guess, it needs to charge at some point. But so that's it. I think that's a really good vision. I think one that's lofty and I dance between whether it's attainable or not, is Elon Musk saying, "We're going to get to Mars." He believes it. He believes it so much that sometimes I'm like, "I guess, we're going to Mars." But then there was the other one of, oh, we want a car that's electric and we want that car to be beautiful so that we will get to a car that's accessible to everyone. And that's kind of followed through. So yeah, I mean, the beautiful things about visions is that it helps you decide it. Is that a work... Do I care about this problem? Is it something I want to do? And then you can take it or leave it.
turns.zh: 绝对地。我特别喜欢的东西，所以我的很多产品思考、产品技巧和工艺，我真的要归功于 Uber。所以当我思考事情时，那里有一些非常神奇的东西。当时我们的价值观之一就是创造魔法。所以我一直遇到“魔法”这个词，但它就是使命，按下按钮，搭车，交通就像流水一样可靠。我以前在尼日利亚，那句标语没有规模化，因为尼日利亚的水不太可靠。所以他们选择了一个稍微更具包容性的版本，即可靠的交通和卫生设施，无处不在，适合每个人，对吗？这就是使命。这并不能真正告诉我，当我到达那里时，图像是什么样子的，但是就像当我每天醒来时，我会想，“我为什么在这家公司工作？”它使每个人在任何地方的交通都变得可靠。 (00:09:12)：稍后我可能会谈论这是如何发生的......我们能够利用它来真正挑战当时的首席执行官特拉维斯·卡兰尼克。我们的愿景是建立一个让您无需停车即可连续旅行的世界。因为城市，平均城市25%是停车位。你在旧金山，你会看到建筑物，只有停车位的楼层，对吧？你会有地下室，仅供停车之用。在一个存在住房问题的世界里，我们的租金价格也高得离谱。试想一下，如果您可以腾出所有这些空间来放置各种东西，对吧？住宅、餐馆，凡是你能想到的。派对，尤其是仓库派对，他们有最好的。这就是愿景。你应该能看到吧？你会说，“哦，我可以看到一个世界。”我的意思是，我住在阿姆斯特丹，我有一辆自行车，我每隔一天就能看到它。他们正在淘汰汽车，实际上将街上的停车场改造成公共花园，对吧？ (00:10:16)：所以这并不疯狂。这是可以实现的。但现在为全世界做这件事，那会是什么样子呢？这就是像 Uber Pool 这样的东西出现的原因，在一个平均汽车载有 1.5 人的世界中，我们可以最大化这一点，然后我们可以实现这种互联的旅行，其中汽车只是移动，然后汽车可能是自动驾驶的，所以你实际上不必驾驶那辆车，所以它不需要停下来。我想，它需要在某个时候充电。但就是这样。我认为这是一个非常好的愿景。我认为埃隆·马斯克（Elon Musk）说的一句话是崇高的，无论是否可以实现，我都会犹豫不决，“我们要去火星。”他相信。他非常相信这一点，有时我会想，“我想，我们要去火星。”但还有另一个，哦，我们想要一辆电动汽车，我们希望那辆车很漂亮，这样我们就能得到一辆每个人都可以使用的汽车。这就是后续的情况。所以，是的，我的意思是，愿景的美妙之处在于它可以帮助你做出决定。那是一份工作吗……我关心这个问题吗？这是我想做的事吗？然后你可以接受或离开它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think with the lofty slash attainable balance, I think that Elon Musk is an interesting example where it may feel impossible, but as an inspirational leader, you almost convince people that it is possible through your confidence and your being in the details, helping people see maybe there's a path. So I think there's an interesting opportunity there to be a leader.
turns.zh: 我认为，通过大幅削减可达到的平衡，我认为埃隆·马斯克是一个有趣的例子，它可能让人感觉不可能，但作为一位鼓舞人心的领导者，你几乎让人们相信，通过你的自信和对细节的关注，这是可能的，帮助人们看到也许有一条路。所以我认为成为领导者有一个有趣的机会。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Yeah. Absolutely.
turns.zh: 是的。绝对地。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: I'll use it an analogy. Let's say we want to go hike. We want to go up to Mount Everest. The vision would be once we're up there, me describing the picture of what we're going to see, we're going to get there, we're going to look around, we'll be the Himalayas, be beautiful, we'll be above the clouds, probably out of breath. That's the vision. It's like I fast-forward into the future, I hold time and I'm in that place and I'm describing the picture, right? And so a city without parking, you can see that, right? And we've all watched sci-fi movies. You can see Mars, Red Planet. So that's the vision and then the mission is the purpose of why we're doing that. We're going to do this to demonstrate that we're able to do it and making sure that we both get there together. It's a very simplistic one, but I'm just giving... That's the purpose. (00:12:46): We're doing it because we want to prove to ourselves that we can summit Mount Everest, which I will not be doing anytime soon, and we're doing it to prove to ourselves something that we can do it and we're capable, and we will do that by making sure that we look out for each other. Because you can get to Mount Everest and not have all the people with you, right? That's a team bonding challenge that I've done once upon a time. It's actually very, very, very intricate and interesting. So that's your vision. And then the mission is the purpose and some set of guiding principles as to what will allow you to achieve that vision.
turns.zh: 我会用它来比喻。假设我们想去徒步旅行。我们想去珠穆朗玛峰。愿景是一旦我们到达那里，我会描述我们将要看到的景象，我们将到达那里，我们将环顾四周，我们将成为喜马拉雅山，变得美丽，我们将在云层之上，可能会喘不过气来。这就是愿景。就好像我快进到未来，我掌握了时间，我就在那个地方，我正在描述那幅画，对吗？所以一个没有停车位的城市，你可以看到这一点，对吧？我们都看过科幻电影。你可以看到火星，红色星球。这就是愿景，而使命就是我们这样做的目的。我们这样做是为了证明我们有能力做到这一点，并确保我们能够共同实现这一目标。这是一个非常简单的问题，但我只是给予……这就是目的。 (00:12:46)：我们这样做是因为我们想向自己证明我们可以登上珠穆朗玛峰，但我不会很快做到这一点，我们这样做是为了向自己证明我们可以做到并且我们有能力，并且我们将通过确保我们互相照顾来做到这一点。因为你可以到达珠穆朗玛峰而不需要所有的人都和你一起，对吗？这是我以前做过的团队凝聚力挑战。它实际上非常非常复杂且有趣。这就是你的愿景。然后使命就是目的和一些指导原则，以帮助您实现这一愿景。

turns.zh: 这真的很方便。这么简单的思考方式......我只是在你说话时做笔记，我完全同意这一点。使命本质上是你存在的原因和原因，以及你的团队斜线公司的目的和愿景……愿景这个词几乎告诉你它是什么。这就是你到达那里时的样子。惊人的。这就是我的真实想法。我将在节目笔记中链接到这篇文章，其中讨论了使命和愿景策略。我会很快给出更多例子。再说一遍，当你在聊天时我把它拉出来只是为了让人们有更多的例子。所以很快就会有几个任务示例。 (00:13:55)：在 Ted，他们的使命是传播思想。他们四处传播思想。 Stripe 的使命是增加互联网的 GDP。宜家的使命是为许多人创造更美好的日常生活。所以我认为这正是你所说的。它们就像我们存在的目的一样？然后是异象。因此，微软的愿景是：每张桌子、每个家庭都有一台电脑。很像我们实现目标后的样子？特斯拉创建了 21 世纪最引人注目的汽车公司。介于两者之间，但我认为已经很接近了。 Lyft，一个城市再次让人感觉很小的世界，交通和科技将人们聚集在一起，而不是分离。多么甜蜜啊。

turns.en: So that's one where it's very warm and fuzzy and I love it. Maybe this is my Uber, but you can see a computer on every desk. That's what I mean by it has to be realistic.

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: So I have a very simplistic framework. I actually don't know who put it together at Uber, but I see as well, one of the most powerful skills of a product manager is storytelling, right? Because you look at generation after generation after generation, what people pass on as stories, they're not numbers, they're not stats, it's stories. And actually when you blend stories with numbers, so if you do numbers alone or numbers with stories or stories alone, the gap is so wide in stories alone. So it's not metrics blended with stories. It's a story, just a pure story. This doesn't mean don't be analytical. So one of the very simplistic tools that I've used, and I use it as well right now at Google, when my team ships the product, I'll put the vision in there to remind what the vision was that they set out to do, right? (00:15:59): And it's once upon a time, write the problem and then write something and then write something, and then one day something happened. And as a result, the state of the world where we're trying to be. It's very simplistic, but in its simplicity of the magic because you are like, "I'm a PM, I'm trying to solve problems." Once upon a time, where were we? Right? It's like what is the thing that we're trying to solve? So I'll give you a simplistic one. I know the team didn't do this for shorts, but the shorts team at YouTube. Once upon a time, YouTube was fun and people had cat videos and zoo and all of that. And then one day it became this really polished thing and a lot of people were producing really polished, very one hour content. And then because of that, a lot of people felt maybe I couldn't create because I can't tell a one-hour story. (00:16:57): And because of that, people decided, okay, I'm just going to watch and consume and not create. And then one day, we launch shorts, 60 seconds, and because of that, anyone can now express themselves again and bring back the joy and magic of YouTube. So it's very simplistic. I'm just using that into the teams who built this. I know this is not your vision, I'm just giving it a story. But I remember this when we did it for Uber as well, we were talking about the loyalty for drivers and some would have this framework and I thought, holy cow, this is it. So that's a very simplistic version. You can go one step up. The one I like to do, and I know that Amazon does this a lot, but as I write... I write an article. I'll write in the headline because if the vision has come to pass, right? And it's gone well, someone's going to be writing hopefully some sexy headline about the thing that you've built. (00:17:54): So I go to the future and I write the headline I would see. And I write the subtitle, just that, and I'll actually use the... I'll [inaudible 00:18:01] it into the page of TechCrunch or [inaudible 00:18:04] or something just so it looks realistic. And I'll put that in the deck just to kind of like, this is where we want to be. And then if I really want to go deep, then I'll write the rest of the article, right? So that's a very simplistic one. Let's stick another version. One that I used, and I show that in a lot of my talks is, I was trying to tell a story when I was at Uber and I was like, "Okay, words are amazing, but a picture tells a thousand words, right?" So I wrote out the thing and I worked with my design partner at the time, and he literally took out a pencil and drew the future. (00:18:37): And the vision I was trying to show was this world where you could walk into any store, any Bodega, mom-and-pop shop, wherever you are in the world, and actually top up your Uber balance, right? So even if you don't have a credit card and you have cash, you can also experience this cashless, seamless Uber experience and that can scale all over the world. And he literally drew a Bodega or does it look like a kiosk, like the ones in Nigeria in my country, you have like a [inaudible 00:19:06]. And then he drew that and you had the person with cash and a receipt just showing your top-up was successful. And we built that product. Not exactly in that way, but we built that product. Sorry, for another day or maybe for later, but that's the story. It took four years to build it, but that image got people so excited about, oh, it's possible. I can see that.
turns.zh: 所以我有一个非常简单的框架。我实际上不知道是谁在 Uber 提出的，但我也看到，产品经理最强大的技能之一就是讲故事，对吧？因为你看着一代又一代人，人们以故事的形式传递的东西，它们不是数字，不是统计数据，而是故事。实际上，当你将故事与数字混合在一起时，如果你单独做数字，或者数字与故事或单独的故事，那么单独的故事中的差距是如此之大。所以它不是与故事混合的指标。这是一个故事，一个纯粹的故事。这并不意味着不要进行分析。因此，我使用过的非常简单的工具之一，我现在在谷歌也使用它，当我的团队交付产品时，我会将愿景放在那里，以提醒他们打算做什么，对吧？ (00:15:59)：从前，写下问题，然后写一些东西，然后写一些东西，然后有一天发生了一些事情。结果就是我们想要成为的世界状况。它非常简单，但在其简单的魔力中，因为你会说，“我是一名产品经理，我正在努力解决问题。”曾几何时，我们在哪里？正确的？就像我们要解决的问题是什么？那么我给你一个简单的。我知道团队这样做并不是为了短片，而是 YouTube 的短片团队。曾几何时，YouTube 很有趣，人们有猫视频和动物园等等。然后有一天，它变成了一件非常精致的事情，很多人都在制作非常精致的、非常一小时的内容。正因为如此，很多人觉得我可能无法创作，因为我无法讲述一小时的故事。 (00:16:57)：正因为如此，人们决定，好吧，我只会观看和消费，而不是创造。然后有一天，我们推出了 60 秒短片，正因为如此，任何人现在都可以再次表达自己，并带回 YouTube 的欢乐和魔力。所以这非常简单。我只是将其用于构建此的团队。我知道这不是你的愿景，我只是给它一个故事。但我记得当我们为 Uber 做这件事时，我们正在谈论司机的忠诚度，有些人会有这个框架，我想，天哪，就是这样。所以这是一个非常简单的版本。你可以再上一层楼。这是我喜欢做的，我知道亚马逊经常这样做，但当我写的时候……我写了一篇文章。我会写在标题中，因为如果愿景已经实现，对吧？一切进展顺利，希望有人会写一些关于你所构建的东西的性感标题。 (00:17:54)：所以我去了未来，写下了我会看到的标题。我写了副标题，就这样，我实际上会使用...我将[听不清 00:18:01] 将其放入 TechCrunch 页面或 [听不清 00:18:04] 或其他东西，这样看起来就很现实。我会把它放在甲板上只是为了有点像，这就是我们想要的地方。然后，如果我真的想深入探讨，那么我会写文章的其余部分，对吧？这是一个非常简单的问题。让我们粘另一个版本。我在很多演讲中都使用过一个，我在 Uber 工作时试图讲一个故事，我当时想，“好吧，文字很棒，但一张图片可以讲述一千个单词，对吗？”所以我写下了这个东西，然后我和当时的设计伙伴一起工作，他真的拿出一支铅笔画出了未来。 (00:18:37)：我试图展示的愿景是，你可以走进任何商店、任何酒窖、夫妻店，无论你身在世界何处，并实际为你的 Uber 余额充值，对吗？因此，即使您没有信用卡但有现金，您也可以体验这种无现金、无缝的 Uber 体验，并且可以扩展到世界各地。他确实画了一个酒窖，或者它看起来像一个亭子，就像我国家尼日利亚的亭子一样，你有一个[听不清00:19:06]。然后他画了那个，你就看到了那个拿着现金和收据的人，表明你的充值成功了。我们开发了该产品。不完全是这样，但我们制造了那个产品。抱歉，改天或者稍后再说，但故事就是这样。它花了四年的时间才建成，但这个形象让人们如此兴奋，哦，这是可能的。我看得出来。

And because of that blank and one day something happened, and that's essentially the vision is like what happened, the big change that you're going to create.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。本质上来说，这是三种传达愿景的方式。第一种是这种Mad Libs 方法，非常简单。那么框架，我们是否可以将人们与您联系起来，您进一步讨论时是否有这个模板？好吧，酷。好吧，酷。因此，在演出笔记中，您会发现一个可以在此处即插即用的小模板，但这个想法曾几何时，一片空白。由于这种空白，有一天发生了一些事情，这本质上就是愿景就像发生的事情一样，你将创造巨大的改变。

I think the press release is... To me, it's dumb to write a press release. No one reads press releases anymore. So I like that you think of it as a TechCrunch article.
turns.zh: 美丽的。这很有趣，它有点跟随英雄的旅程，就像今天的世界，然后这是你遇到的问题和你必须克服的挑战。然后这就是我们如何击败敌人的。然后我们又回到了默认世界。好的，这是一条路。另一条路是写作，逆向工作的方法，写一篇文章。我认为新闻稿是......对我来说，写新闻稿是愚蠢的。没有人再阅读新闻稿了。所以我喜欢你将其视为一篇 TechCrunch 文章。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something you remember where you did that actually with a product? Like you wrote an article of a product you were launching?
turns.zh: 您是否还记得您在产品中实际执行过哪些操作？就像您写了一篇关于您要推出的产品的文章一样？

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: At Uber, we were talking about cars, then it was like, well push a button, get a ride. It could be push a button, go anywhere. And so, one of the things I started talking about... And this was the beauty of Uber, it allowed you kind of challenge the status quo. I started pushing this idea of if we need to have this more multimodal trip where I could take a... Ride a bicycle or a scooter, then I get to the train station, buy my ticket, scan in. Then from there I go into an Uber maybe then I come out and the other end and I get a scooter, whatever that is. It's this connected single trip. And the reason I was doing that was I was a Platform PM and surprise surprise, I always say Platform PMs, you have to be an order of magnitude even more stronger I think at vision setting because you have to build the foundations of stuff you don't even know is coming. (00:22:03): So I would do these exercises with my partner teams to figure out, even if they don't know it, force a vision out of them just to say, "Is this where we are going?" Because then as somebody building the commerce infrastructure for Uber, I need to know when I need to build if that is a scenario that's actually going to happen. And we were also thinking about this world where you could tap to pay with your Uber phone. So there were all these crazy ideas and I wrote a headline of Uber really wants to replace your... I put it as your clipper card in San Francisco. Because I wanted my San Francisco buddies to relate to what I was saying. So I was like, "Uber is now replacing your Clipper card. All you need is your phone and the app." And I wrote it out and we didn't go and build that product, but we built the payments and commerce infrastructure for the team that did. And we were very involved at the beginning when it was getting kicked off of how does this look in a world where you can use your Uber to pay for transport? You can do that today. So yeah, that's a real life example.
turns.zh: 在 Uber，我们谈论的是汽车，然后就像是，按下按钮，搭车。只需按一下按钮，就可以去任何地方。所以，我开始谈论的一件事......这就是 Uber 的美妙之处，它允许你挑战现状。我开始推动这个想法，如果我们需要更多的多式联运旅行，我可以骑自行车或踏板车，然后我到达火车站，买票，扫描。然后从那里我进入优步，也许然后我出来，在另一端，我得到一辆踏板车，无论那是什么。这是一次连贯的单程旅行。我这样做的原因是我是一名平台产品经理，令人惊讶的是，我总是说平台产品经理，我认为在愿景设定方面，你必须要强大一个数量级，因为你必须为你甚至不知道即将到来的东西打下基础。 (00:22:03)：因此，我会与我的合作伙伴团队一起进行这些练习，以找出答案（即使他们不知道），迫使他们产生愿景，只是说：“这是我们要去的地方吗？”因为作为为 Uber 构建商业基础设施的人，我需要知道何时需要构建这种情况是否真的会发生。我们也在考虑这个世界，你可以用你的优步手机点击支付。因此，出现了所有这些疯狂的想法，我写了一个标题：Uber 真的想取代你的......我把它作为你在旧金山的 Clipper 卡。因为我希望我的旧金山朋友能理解我所说的。所以我当时想，“Uber 现在正在更换你的 Clipper 卡。你所需要的只是你的手机和应用程序。”我把它写出来，我们没有去构建该产品，但我们为团队构建了支付和商业基础设施。我们一开始就非常积极地参与其中，当时我们正在思考，在一个可以使用 Uber 支付交通费用的世界里，这会是什么样子？今天你就可以做到。是的，这是一个现实生活中的例子。

turns.zh: 您认为这样做会产生什么影响？您认为转发这篇文章有哪些好处？您是否有过这样的回忆：哇，这真的很有帮助？

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: It's two things. So you'll hear me say product management is clarity and conviction. And in writing the headline, you have to focus. Headline is not like... It's not a PRD, right? It's a headline. So when I've done this, what is the impact of this going to be? What's the feeling [inaudible 00:23:56] people with? And it forces you to get to that clarity of, okay, we solved this problem. This is actually going to be the painkiller that we're solving. And then they translate that pain dealer into, they have a headache, they no longer have a headache. Do you know what I mean? So I think it breaks clarity. So for me, as the PM I'm like, this is why I'm saying this is important. Then you have the subtitled. So they'll usually have the headline and I'm like, sub bit. They've just launched a way to something something, and you have to write that as well. (00:24:22): What is the thing we're launching and is that realistic? And then using that to kind of socialize the idea to say, "This actually could work, right?" And I didn't go off and build it. Somebody else went and did it, but we had already thought about it and bit that into our platform vision of we need to be able to support these different kinds of ways to pay. There's another interesting one that you're going to go to. The third one, which is write the story. Write the article that someone else will write or visualize it, right? And the visualize it, two things actually happened. One a year and a half ago, in a strategy session I was running at YouTube, i...
turns.zh: 这是两件事。所以你会听到我说产品管理是清晰和坚定的。在写标题时，你必须集中注意力。标题不像……这不是 PRD，对吧？这是一个标题。那么当我这样做时，会产生什么影响？ [听不清 00:23:56] 人们有什么感觉？它迫使你清楚地认识到，好吧，我们解决了这个问题。这实际上将成为我们正在解决的止痛药。然后他们将痛苦经销商翻译成，他们头痛，他们不再头痛。你知道我的意思吗？所以我认为这打破了清晰度。所以对我来说，作为总理，这就是为什么我说这很重要。然后你就有了字幕。所以他们通常会有标题，我想，小一点。他们刚刚推出了一种实现某事的方法，你也必须写下来。 (00:24:22)：我们正在推出什么东西，它现实吗？然后用它来社交化这个想法，说：“这实际上可行，对吧？”我并没有去建造它。其他人已经这么做了，但我们已经考虑过这一点，并将其纳入我们的平台愿景中，即我们需要能够支持这些不同类型的支付方式。你要去的还有另一个有趣的地方。第三个，就是写故事。写别人会写的文章或将其想象出来，对吗？想象一下，实际上发生了两件事。一年半前，在我在 YouTube 举办的一次战略会议上，我...

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: The strategy session I was running at YouTube, I actually took a screenshot of the Google Play Store. I mean, I use an iPhone, but I worked at Google, so I was trying to be... So I took the Google Play Store and then I created rounded rectangles, just blank rectangles, four panels. And then I printed that out and I gave everyone a sheet and I said, "If we solve these problems, we solve all these problems that we've identified, what would be the screenshots?" (00:25:32): You know when you go on the app store, it has the make money or express yourself, what are we trying to say and what is the mock, the hero mock, the marquee mock that we're showing? And then again, it forces people to, oh goodness, we can't show everything, so it's got to be three or four things that land the big rocks that will solve this problem. Right? So everyone did theirs and then we talked about it and what was interesting is you'll find two or three that everyone comes up with if you've done a good job of telling a story around the problems. And it actually quite beautiful to see. So that's a very simplistic visualization that's not like a beautiful sketch or video.
turns.zh: 我在 YouTube 上举办的策略会议实际上截取了 Google Play 商店的屏幕截图。我的意思是，我使用 iPhone，但我在 Google 工作，所以我试图……所以我使用了 Google Play 商店，然后创建了圆角矩形、空白矩形、四个面板。然后我把它打印出来，给每个人一张纸，我说，“如果我们解决这些问题，我们解决我们已经发现的所有这些问题，屏幕截图会是什么？” (00:25:32)：你知道当你进入应用商店时，它可以赚钱或表达自己，我们想说什么，我们展示的模拟是什么，英雄模拟，字幕模拟是什么？话又说回来，它迫使人们，天哪，我们无法展示一切，所以必须有三到四件事才能解决这个问题。正确的？所以每个人都做了他们的，然后我们讨论了它，有趣的是，如果你很好地围绕问题讲述了一个故事，你会发现每个人都会提出两三个。它实际上看起来很漂亮。所以这是一个非常简单的可视化，不像漂亮的草图或视频。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that as just a reminder that when you're even the article approach of announcing the thing instead of the traditional press release or even a Tech Wrench article, it's where will people find out about the thing you've built, and then use that as a way to frame what you've done. So in your case, it's like the app store. They're going to see this update in the app store. Let's just see what that would look like as we announce it in the app store. Could end up being a tweet, could end up being podcasts. There's all these different channels. So I think that gives people more ways of telling the story. If it's not going to be a press release. (00:26:41): Then yeah, so you talked about this third approach of mocking up essentially the vision. I always feel like if you have a designer helping you craft your vision, it's such a unfair advantage. So definitely try to a rope a designer in to help you tell a story.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这一点，它只是提醒您，当您以文章的方式而不是传统的新闻稿甚至是 Tech Wrench 文章来宣布该事物时，人们将在哪里找到您所构建的事物，然后将其用作框架您所做的事情的一种方式。所以就你而言，它就像应用程序商店。他们将在应用商店中看到此更新。让我们看看当我们在应用商店中发布它时会是什么样子。最终可能成为推文，也可能成为播客。有所有这些不同的渠道。所以我认为这给了人们更多讲述故事的方式。如果这不是新闻稿。 (00:26:41)：那么，是的，你谈到了模拟愿景的第三种方法。我总觉得如果有设计师帮助你打造你的愿景，这是一种不公平的优势。所以一定要尝试让设计师来帮助你讲故事。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because just one design is going to, like you said, worth a thousand words, as they say.
turns.zh: 因为正如他们所说，正如您所说，仅仅一个设计就值得一千个字。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: The thing though is I feel like it's an easy cop out to be like, "Oh, but my design team doesn't have resources." So I'm like, "No, that's not an excuse. Start drawing it with your hands in the app store." Still tell the story because the story, you should be able to tell this. I'm obsessed with Steve Jobs. He would say, "Tell the story without slides." Right? So that mocking it up is just so you can actually bring that narrative and tell that story. And do an app store or sketch it out or use little rectangles to show low fidelity mocks. Do not use, I don't have a designer, to be the excuse for why you don't bring it to life.
turns.zh: 但问题是，我觉得“哦，但我的设计团队没有资源”很容易逃避。所以我想，“不，这不是借口。开始在应用商店里用手画吧。”还是讲故事吧，因为故事，你应该能讲这个。我对史蒂夫·乔布斯很着迷。他会说，“不用幻灯片讲故事。”正确的？因此，模拟它只是为了让你能够真正地叙述并讲述那个故事。并创建一个应用程序商店或绘制草图或使用小矩形来显示低保真度模拟。不要用“我没有设计师”作为你不把它变成现实的借口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And often the designer sees it and like, "This sucks. I'm going to make it better."
turns.zh: 设计师经常看到它并喜欢，“这太糟糕了。我要让它变得更好。”

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Exactly. So that's exactly what I did. I sketched this thing once and I gave it to a designer. It was literally post-it notes and they were like, "Okay, I see where you're going and it's exciting. I have some cycles, I'll spin it up." They spun up a lo-fi one, loved it, and I'm like, "Actually, I'm just going to make it pretty." Then they made it pretty and we got there. I mean now I'm a director, so I have a bit more agency with resources, but I was like a L-four PM, not even a senior PM when I did my first vision exercise.
turns.zh: 确切地。这正是我所做的。我画了一次这个东西的草图，然后把它交给了设计师。这实际上是便利贴，他们就像是，“好吧，我知道你要去哪里，这很令人兴奋。我有一些周期，我会旋转它。”他们制作了一款低保真的产品，很喜欢它，我想，“实际上，我只是想让它变得漂亮。”然后他们把它做得很漂亮，我们就到了那里。我的意思是，现在我是一名董事，所以我拥有更多的资源和代理权，但当我进行第一次愿景练习时，我就像一个 L-4 PM，甚至不是高级 PM。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, this is awesome because I think it's really vague, this idea of I need to develop a vision, and I think you've shared some incredibly tactical clear steps you can take. I also want to talk about how to actually develop the vision. I think you have kind of this step-by-step approach. Is that right?
turns.zh: 好吧，这太棒了，因为我认为这真的很模糊，我需要制定一个愿景，而且我认为您已经分享了一些可以采取的令人难以置信的战术明确步骤。我还想谈谈如何实际发展愿景。我认为你有这种循序渐进的方法。是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. So before we get to that, just again reminding people what we just talked about, which is just like here's all these ways of framing your vision, and there's a lot of ways to do it. It's not like you need to make a beautiful deck that you can just write it out. You could write a press release, you could write a tweet or you could get a designer help you mock it up or just mock it up yourself. Awesome. Okay, so let's talk about your suggestions of how to actually go about developing and figuring out the vision for your product.
turns.zh: 好吧，太棒了。因此，在我们开始之前，再次提醒人们我们刚才谈到的内容，就像这里有所有这些构建愿景的方法，并且有很多方法可以实现。这并不像你需要制作一个漂亮的套牌，然后你就可以把它写出来。你可以写一篇新闻稿，你可以写一条推文，或者你可以让设计师帮助你模拟它，或者你自己模拟它。惊人的。好的，让我们谈谈您对如何实际开发和确定产品愿景的建议。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Yeah. There are three pieces if you think about it. So one is what I call empathize. The second is create. So we spend a lot of time talking about create, the middle piece. Another's evangelize. And so I empathize with the customer, the problem. I put myself in their shoes. I really get a visual understanding of what those problems are. I'll talk about it in a second the tactical way I have done that across Uber, Netflix, and Google in a way that scales. Then the create piece where it's okay, now we've solved this problem. What does the world look like? That's the vision we've just been talking about. And then finally, evangelize. (00:29:36): So I find just especially as you get more senior, the life cycle of a product or a group of products gets wider and wider and wider. And so I set out a vision, for example at YouTube last year that was called Vision 2026. And only this year, a year and a half later, are we now at a stage where it's actually going into the planning cycle. We've actually finished all the things were already in progress. We're actually now funding some of the big rocks that get us there. (00:30:08): So there's a bit of patience that comes with it. And I think some people just give up when they get to the stage because you're going to meet a lot of naysayers. That one person's like, "But there's no way the engineering is ever going to solve." There's always going to be those people which is why I said you need to come up with a vision that's in a vacuum of the technical limitations because the limitations of today might not be the limitations of tomorrow. (00:30:32): So going back to the empathize, one of my peers at work uses this word, he says, "You need to do understand work." And what is understand work? It's crazy to me the number of PMs who never go through their products and go through the... unless of course you're the onboarding PM, but actually go through the onboarding flow. Because we're all in this state of using the product. But actually, that first step where I don't have the product, what does that look like? I have multiple variations of accounts on YouTube. I have multiple accounts on Instagram. I have multiple accounts on Tiktok where I'm just using the product just like how does it manifest? What do I like? What's going well? I had this thing with Uber. I had Uber, I had other partner apps, I would look at them and payment services, empathize comes very easily if you dog food and then cat food. Dog food, meaning using your own product, absolutely a must. Cat food using your competitors or other people in the landscape's products. (00:31:36): So that's one piece. The other piece is obviously research, but research is an interesting one because I think you use research. I think research is rich when it's giving you foundational problems that are a couple of cycles out, obviously depending on the level of research you're doing. But your researcher, if you think about the product cycle, research is ahead, and then UX, and then you go into building, it's like in that phase. (00:32:06): And so I find too many people lean into and, "Let's go test it, let's go do some research." It's like, dude, you're a human. Look at the products. Would you use that? You built some intuition from just exposing yourself to really good products. Every time you pick up your phone, what is it about the apps that you love? Do you think about that? Oh, I open up my phone. I love Spotify. I also love YouTube Music, but I really love Spotify for my music. I've used it for years and I'm like, okay, what is it about this new thing that just rolled that I love? And I try to articulate that. (00:32:44): So there's that piece, but then the tactical thing that I almost make every PM on my team do I call it top 10 things you should know. It's a living document. So in my org right now I've got quite a number of PMs and for each of those PMs in this living Google Doc, it's like go slash studio problems, they literally put 10 things, like 10 problems you should know. And you revise it. Every quarter you update it and they're separate. So it's like a living set of problems. And they could be qualitative, they could be quantitative, they could be tech debt. They should be tech debt.
turns.zh: 是的。如果你仔细想想的话，可以分为三部分。所以其中之一就是我所说的同理心。二是创造。所以我们花了很多时间谈论创造，中间的部分。另一个人传福音。所以我对客户和问题表示同情。我设身处地为他们着想。我真正直观地了解了这些问题是什么。我稍后会讨论我在 Uber、Netflix 和 Google 上以可扩展的方式做到这一点的战术方式。然后创建一块就可以了，现在我们已经解决了这个问题。世界是什么样子的？这就是我们刚才谈到的愿景。最后，传福音。 (00:29:36)：所以我发现，尤其是当你的级别越来越高时，一个产品或一组产品的生命周期会变得越来越宽。因此，我去年在 YouTube 上提出了一个愿景，称为“愿景 2026”。直到今年，也就是一年半之后，我们现在才真正进入规划周期。我们实际上已经完成了所有已经在进行的事情。事实上，我们现在正在资助一些让我们实现这一目标的大石头。 (00:30:08)：因此需要一点耐心。我认为有些人一上台就放弃了，因为你会遇到很多反对者。有人会说，“但是工程永远无法解决这个问题。”总会有这样的人，这就是为什么我说你需要在技术限制的真空中提出一个愿景，因为今天的限制可能不会是明天的限制。 (00:30:32)：回到同理心，我的一位同事用了这个词，他说，“你需要理解工作。”什么是理解工作？对我来说，有很多 PM 从来没有浏览过他们的产品，也没有经历过……当然，除非你是入职 PM，但实际上经历了入职流程，这对我来说很疯狂。因为我们都处于这种使用产品的状态。但实际上，第一步我没有产品，那是什么样子的？我在 YouTube 上有多种帐户。我在 Instagram 上有多个帐户。我在 Tiktok 上有多个帐户，我只是在使用该产品，就像它如何体现一样？我喜欢什么？进展顺利吗？我和 Uber 发生过这样的事。我有 Uber，我有其他合作伙伴应用程序，我会查看它们和支付服务，如果你先吃狗粮，然后再吃猫粮，那么很容易产生共鸣。狗粮，意味着使用自己的产品，绝对是必须的。猫粮使用你的竞争对手或景观中其他人的产品。 (00:31:36)：所以这是一件。另一部分显然是研究，但研究是一个有趣的部分，因为我认为你使用研究。我认为当研究给你几个周期后的基础问题时，研究就很丰富，这显然取决于你正在进行的研究水平。但是你的研究人员，如果你考虑产品周期，研究就在前面，然后是用户体验，然后你进入构建，就像在那个阶段一样。 (00:32:06)：所以我发现太多人倾向于“让我们去测试一下，让我们去做一些研究。”就像，伙计，你是一个人。看看产品。你会用那个吗？通过接触真正好的产品，你建立了一些直觉。每次你拿起手机时，你喜欢的应用程序有哪些？你想一想吗？哦，我打开手机。我喜欢 Spotify。我也喜欢 YouTube Music，但我更喜欢 Spotify 来听音乐。我已经使用它很多年了，我想，好吧，这个我喜欢的新东西到底是什么？我试图阐明这一点。 (00:32:44)：那就是那件事，但是我几乎让团队中的每个 PM 都做的战术事情我称之为你应该知道的 10 件事。这是一份活的文件。因此，现在在我的组织中，我有相当多的 PM，对于这个活生生的 Google 文档中的每一个 PM，这就像 golash studio 问题一样，他们实际上提出了 10 件事，就像你应该知道的 10 个问题。然后你修改它。每个季度你都会更新它并且它们是分开的。所以这就像一系列活生生的问题。它们可以是定性的，也可以是定量的，也可以是科技债务。它们应该是科技债务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are just known problems with the product that everyone was aware of?
turns.zh: 这些只是每个人都知道的产品的已知问题吗？

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Awesome.
turns.zh: 好的。惊人的。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: You kind of farm for the problems. So you keep that doc going. And so I first started this at Uber on the money team and I called it money problems, more money, more problems because I do fundamentally believe we should bring joy into everything we try to do, so have fun with it. So more money, more problems. And essentially, it was in partnership with my data scientist partners that he had a team of product analysts and data scientists and they would pair up with my PMs and we would have the UX team, the UXR team, the data team, and the product managers, and engineering get together and actually look at their problems. (00:34:09): So that living document means that for me, if I go around at least my minus one, not just for me but my engineering partner's minus ones, and my design partner's minus ones, and we chat them and say, "What are the top five problems for studio?" They should all have the same answer. This says I've done my job because then we all know the problems. You can debate them. You can discuss them. You can have sessions where you revise and review them. But we do that and then we go into a room and for example at Uber, I literally printed them on cards and I put them on tables, scattered the groups and had people discuss and vote the ones that is the most painful because then you see the whole thing. (00:34:52): So that's the empathize bit. I'm spending a lot of time on this because I can't tell you how many times the clarity of the problem, going back to clarity and conviction, is missing and that problem is kind of like the North star. Everything's going on, but there's a north star that doesn't move.
turns.zh: 你可以说是为了解决问题而耕种。所以你让那个医生继续下去。因此，我首先在 Uber 的资金团队中开始了这项工作，我称之为金钱问题，更多的钱，更多的问题，因为我从根本上相信我们应该为我们尝试做的每件事带来快乐，所以享受其中的乐趣。所以钱越多，问题就越多。从本质上讲，正是与我的数据科学家合作伙伴合作，他拥有了一个由产品分析师和数据科学家组成的团队，他们将与我的产品经理配对，我们将拥有 UX 团队、UXR 团队、数据团队、产品经理和工程人员，他们聚集在一起，实际研究他们的问题。 (00:34:09)：所以这个动态文档对我来说意味着，如果我至少解决我的负一问题，不仅是我自己，还有我的工程合作伙伴的负一问题，以及我的设计合作伙伴的负一问题，我们和他们聊天并说：“工作室面临的五个首要问题是什么？”他们应该都有相同的答案。这表明我已经完成了我的工作，因为那时我们都知道问题所在。你可以辩论它们。您可以讨论它们。您可以召开会议来修改和审查它们。但我们这样做，然后我们进入一个房间，例如在 Uber，我把它们打印在卡片上，然后把它们放在桌子上，分散小组，让人们讨论和投票那些最痛苦的，因为然后你就会看到整个事情。 (00:34:52)：这就是共情位。我在这个问题上花了很多时间，因为我无法告诉你有多少次问题的清晰度（回到清晰度和信念）缺失，而这个问题有点像北极星。一切都在发生，但有一颗北极星不动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before you move on, there's so much there I just want to touch on that are really interesting insights. One is just this point you're making of when you're trying to develop a vision or thinking about the next step, you should be way ahead of that. You have this doc that you've been working on and consistently update and it's there way ahead of time. It's not like cool, next year's coming up, let's start from scratch and figure out what the vision is long-term. (00:35:32): Two is there's this quote that I think Patrick Hollison tweeted that I always think about in these discussions where a lot of people think of user research. It's like user research, often people think of user research, you do user research and that tells you what to do. turns.zh: 在继续之前，我只想谈谈非常有趣的见解。其中之一就是当你试图制定愿景或考虑下一步时你所提出的这一点，你应该走在前面。您拥有这份一直在编写并不断更新的文档，而且它已经提前发布了。这并不酷，明年即将到来，让我们从头开始，弄清楚长期愿景是什么。 (00:35:32)：第二，我认为帕特里克·霍利森 (Patrick Hollison) 在推特上引用了这句话，在这些讨论中，很多人都想到了用户研究，我一直在思考这句话。这就像用户研究，人们通常会想到用户研究，你进行用户研究，然后告诉你该做什么。他提出了这一点，不，应该是用户研究更新你的客户心智模型，他们需要什么，他们遇到的问题，你正在写的股票，然后这个心智模型告诉你要构建什么。 (00:35:57)：所以我认为这是一个很大的区别，它与您所说的“应该相信自己的直觉和判断力”相关。很多人认为作为产品经理我不应该有任何意见。我只是想听听数据和研究告诉我什么。我不会试图让团队产生偏见，但随着时间的推移，我越来越多地了解到，你应该真正相信自己的直觉和直觉，正如你所说的那样。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: If I could put all the research into Bard or ChatGPT and it could spit out a PRD, then you haven't done your job. So basically I maybe panicked my team. I came in, I'm like, gen AI, everybody's talking about all the stuff that you do with creating content, but what I want you to think about is what is the value add you bring that I can't just put into an AI right now and say, "Tell me the big thing based on this research that exists." And I think that's the thing that people undervalue a lot. (00:37:25): It's like you start program managing and just spitting out what engineering said we can't do and UX said they could do and you become this. That's not the job. It's like you're curating those problems together.
turns.zh: 如果我可以将所有研究放入 Bard 或 ChatGPT 并且它可以输出 PRD，那么你还没有完成你的工作。所以基本上我可能让我的团队感到恐慌。我进来的时候，我想，人工智能时代，每个人都在谈论你在创建内容时所做的所有事情，但我希望你思考的是你带来的附加值是什么，我现在不能只是将其放入人工智能中并说，“告诉我基于现有研究的重要事情。” (00:36:49)：所以我从未听过帕特里克·霍利森说过这句话，但我同意。这是正确的。我认为这就是当你考虑产品经理的素质时，我认为有四个支柱：产品意识、领导力、执行承诺和技术能力。这不是产品逻辑。这是产品感..这是一种感觉，对吗？这是一种正确的感觉，随着时间的推移，对产品的接触和好奇心会完善这种感觉。我认为这就是人们低估的事情。 (00:37:25)：这就像你开始项目管理，只是吐出工程部门说我们不能做的事情，用户体验部门说他们可以做的事情，然后你就变成了这样。那不是工作。我们的工作就是清晰明确，将这种背景真正带入正在解决的一系列问题中，然后将它们一起解决。这就是关键。就像你们一起解决这些问题一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny

(00:38:04): Okay, so just to summarize some of the tips you've shared on this empathize step. turns.zh: 作为一名产品经理，我发现的挑战之一是让人们相信你的直觉，知道为什么这是正确的。但我认为这又回到了愿景的力量，帮助每个人保持一致，就像这就是我们存在的原因，这就是我们要去的地方，这就是我感觉可能是一个机会。 (00:38:04)：好的，总结一下您在同理心步骤中分享的一些技巧。一是基本上是用户研究，但我认为更重要的是，用它来帮助您了解用户遇到的问题以及他们的需求等。你们还谈了什么？哦，使用产品。实际上是该产品的用户。在你的情况下，就像上传 YouTube 视频一样。是的。还有别的吗？好的，这是您分享的文档。太棒了。所以基本上只是我们的用户在使用我们的产品时遇到的已知问题的运行文档。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Correct. And when you start getting to the strategic lens, so you have a set of problems, what I sometimes will do is especially if you're, for example a platform PM, PMs generally have lots of stakeholders, there'll be a marketing team that's asking for something or an operations team that's like our market needs this. I'll sometimes bring them in at the beginning of the strategy session and give them a template, 10 things you should know. So you use my framework to give me 10 problems. Because if you say, "Come present," they'll do like 50 slides. No, that's just 10 things you should know and stack rank them. So I put the work on you now to give me some color. (00:39:14): I hear from marketing, comm, support, research, content strategy. Actually had that in my last strategy session where it was the most mind-blowing 10 things you should know. One of them was like the average reading age of an American is 11 years old. And so you start to think of, oh my god, all the text we have, maybe we should use images or a video or whatever. (00:39:50): So that would be the tactical if you want to take it to a more strategic lens. That's how I'd run the first day of my strategy session is usually insights. turns.zh: 正确的。当你开始进入战略视角时，你会遇到一系列问题，我有时会做的特别是如果你是平台 PM，PM 通常有很多利益相关者，会有一个营销团队要求某些东西或一个运营团队，就像我们的市场需要这个一样。有时我会在策略会议开始时让他们进来，并给他们一个模板，即你应该知道的 10 件事。所以你用我的框架给我出了10个问题。因为如果你说“来吧”，他们就会播放 50 张幻灯片。不，这只是您应该了解的 10 件事，并对它们进行排名。所以我现在把工作交给你来给我一些色彩。 (00:39:14)：我听到了营销、传播、支持、研究、内容策略的意见。事实上，在我上次的策略会议中，这是你应该知道的最令人兴奋的 10 件事。其中之一就像美国人的平均阅读年龄是11岁。所以你开始思考，天哪，我们拥有的所有文本，也许我们应该使用图像或视频或其他什么。因此，对问题进行这种多方面的看法，然后你对核心问题进行打磨，然后你就得到了最后的 10 个。 (00:39:50)：如果你想从更具战略性的角度来看，这将是战术。这就是我第一天战略会议的方式，通常是洞察。我通常会花三天时间，先是洞察、策略，然后是大石头。洞察部分是我们深入研究问题的地方，我使用这个你应该知道的 10 件事的模板，然后我们得出你应该知道的 10 件事的最终列表，就像一个综合列表。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like this additional tip you just shared of as you're trying to develop a vision for a team is bring in stakeholders and use this framework to help them crystallize here's the most important things to me from the product and things that I think are big opportunities. Okay, so this week of work you just shared, so can you just talk a bit more about this? Is this you leading the team through an exercise to develop a vision and a strategy?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢你刚刚分享的这个额外的技巧，因为你正在尝试为团队制定一个愿景，即引入利益相关者并使用这个框架来帮助他们具体化产品中对我来说最重要的事情以及我认为是巨大机会的事情。从本质上讲，现在你已经得到了利益相关者的支持，嘿，至少他们听到了我的意见，他们理解了，然后这就是他们想出的办法。然后我可能会说，“不，但是这个东西怎么样？”这至少为您提供了一种将每个人聚集在一起并了解流程进展情况的方法。好的，您刚刚分享了本周的工作，您能多谈谈吗？这是您带领团队通过练习来制定愿景和战略吗？

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: Correct. Correct.
turns.zh: 正确的。正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. And so you said the first three days are aligning and fully understanding and immersing yourself in insights?

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: I usually have strategy sessions of three days. I've tried to do it in two days. That is the absolute limit because I think you need to create white space for just the magic to happen. But I usually use a framework that it's literally what I call the narrative structure. So when we get into the conviction part, the clarity is the problems to solve. The conviction is the narrative. The framing of that conviction is insights, strategy, big rocks. (00:41:29): So the insights day is just focused on understand work, these five problems, actually using the app, doing teardowns of other apps. It's just like a day of understanding. So the Google design, they ask the experts. In a way I've given the experts a template, that's what I'm doing basically. And then the second day is where we now go into the strategy of all the problems we've seen, the 10, which are the ones we want to focus on in which order?
turns.zh: 我通常会进行为期三天的策略会议。我已经尝试在两天内做到这一点。这是绝对的限制，因为我认为你需要创造空白才能让魔法发生。但我通常使用一个框架，字面上就是我所说的叙事结构。因此，当我们进入信念部分时，清晰度就是要解决的问题。信念就是叙述。这一信念的框架是洞察力、战略和大石头。 (00:41:29)：所以洞察日的重点是理解工作、这五个问题、实际使用该应用程序、拆解其他应用程序。这就像理解的一天。所以Google设计的时候，他们请教了专家。在某种程度上，我给了专家一个模板，这就是我基本上正在做的事情。然后第二天我们将讨论我们所看到的所有问题的策略，这 10 个问题是我们希望按什么顺序关注的？

turns.en: And who's in these meetings?
turns.zh: 谁参加了这些会议？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So it's the leaders of the team.
turns.zh: 知道了。所以这是团队的领导者。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: The leaders of the team. And depending on the org, I'll bring in data science because at Google we have a more shared data science resource. So I'll usually invite them as one of the partners. Come tell 10 things you should know. So they'll say, "We need to do more instrumentation," or whatever. (00:42:31): But you hit on the fantastic point which I was going to connect later, which is when you get to the evangelized stage, humans love to know you heard them. So imagine it's like you did all the work of bringing them together to say, "Hey, tell me 10 things." It's like we heard you and then we parse them into these 10 and everybody agreed with these 10 and therefore that's why we came up with this solution.
turns.zh: 团队的领导者。根据组织的不同，我将引入数据科学，因为在谷歌，我们拥有更多共享的数据科学资源。所以我通常会邀请他们作为合作伙伴之一。来告诉你你应该知道的10件事。所以他们会说，“我们需要做更多的仪器”，或者其他什么。 (00:42:31)：但是你说到了我稍后要提到的一个奇妙的点，那就是当你到达福音传播阶段时，人们喜欢知道你听到了他们的声音。因此，想象一下，就像您完成了所有工作，将他们聚集在一起说：“嘿，告诉我 10 件事。”你提出了问题，然后回来说：“这是我们要关注的战略，这是愿景。”你传福音的最后阶段变得容易多了，因为这就像你是如何达到这个异象的？这件事就这样消失了，但你们并没有解决这个问题。就像我们听到了您的声音，然后我们将它们解析为这 10 个，每个人都同意这 10 个，因此这就是我们提出这个解决方案的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's segue to the evangelize step, which I think I always talk about. I always think about the Seinfeld meme of when he is trying to get a car reservation where he shows up and they don't have his car and they're like, "We have your reservation, we just don't have your car." And he's like, "That's the most important part of the reservation. You take the reservation, but you don't keep the reservation. That's the most important part." So I think to me it's always like you have this vision, you have amazing roadmap strategy, but if no one even knows it or hears it, that's the most important part. So I think it's super important to understand this. So I'd love to hear your advice on just how to successfully evangelize and share this vision that you've come up with.
turns.zh: 那么让我们继续进行传福音的步骤，我想我一直在谈论这一点。我总是想起《宋飞正传》中的模因，当他试图预订汽车时，他出现了，但他们没有他的车，他们就像是，“我们有你的预订，我们只是没有你的车。”他说，“这是预订中最重要的部分。你接受预订，但你不保留预订。这是最重要的部分。”所以我认为对我来说，你总是有这样的愿景，你有令人惊叹的路线图策略，但如果没有人知道或听到它，那就是最重要的部分。所以我认为理解这一点非常重要。因此，我很想听听您关于如何成功传播福音并分享您提出的愿景的建议。

turns.speaker: Ebi Atawodi
turns.en: In terms of evangelizing, I think about three concentric circles. So the core of your vision is your team. And I want to make sure my team understands the vision because I'm basically saying, "Get on this boat, we're sailing to the vision of the Bermuda or some island," and I describe this beautiful island. They kind of have to be bought in and have conviction that they want to get there to actually sail on that boat together. (00:44:20): And so the team is the biggest part and it's the whole team. It's not like just the PMs are the vision. We're just the designers are the vision. I will literally first start with each of the folks that were in the room. We will basically bring our teams together and present an app. So for example, the one we did last year, we presented to what we call studio leads, which are essentially the triads for each of the product team, PM, engineering, and design for each of the product teams, and just presented it out. And I had multiple. (00:44:50): We had the first one. Then I had one in my PM weekly, presented it again then, "Hey folks, still any questions?" Because people are still... It's percolating. It's like the tea bag. It's oozing out. They're trying to understand it and they're trying to stress test it. And what I also do is I write the output of the workshop. So I'll always write the output. These are the insights we came out with. Here's the ones upon a time framework. Here's the strategy. Here are the big rocks and a vision is coming. (00:45:18): And then we'll do the vision and say, "But this is the vision of where we're going if we do all these things." And that will be a living document, comments, open for comments, no edit, not view only, comments because you want anyone to leave comments in there and just feel they have a say. You don't have to respond to all of them. You don't have to resolve all of them, but just if you put rocks in a washing machine, they polish each other. I like this friction. (00:45:47): I always like, I go into the forest, I cut a piece of wood, and our job together is to polish it down to the beautiful danish furniture. So it's okay to have that friction to do that for a bit. And then once the team has kind of gotten to a place, I'm not trying to get anyone to a hundred percent certainty, I'm trying to get you just on the ride. They will come, right? (00:46:05): Then I kind of go to this next layer, which is the stakeholders, those people that came in and their teams and their managers go to them and sort of get them brought in to the vision as well. And they'll also bring perspectives, right? You're missing this piece. We have a lot of engineering. Support tickets will blow up if you do this thing. What does that look like? You guys haven't solved the thing we need to do today. You're talking about something five years out. (00:46:32): You're going to get all the variations of feedback. That's okay. The core that people have bought into that story. And it's okay to have all the... And then finally, once you've got the feedback from stakeholders, you then go to leadership, and leadership really as high as possible. So when I was at Uber and I was like an L-five, L-six, I had visions going all the way. I mean I had a fantastic leader. He put me on stage at an all hands to present the vision. And we were like one wallet, all Uber experiences. And then we have this vision of a world where Uber Eats, it could be trains, it could be whatever and you have this one Uber wallet that can be used for all of them. And we had mocks of what that looked like. (00:47:13): So go as big as possible. Go big. Let people tell you to pull back. Let your manager use lasso and pull you back. Go as much as possible. So I go to leadership and then I have leadership, I have to find that story as much as possible. So those are the three concentric circles. turns.zh: 在传福音方面，我想到了三个同心圆。所以你的愿景的核心是你的团队。我想确保我的团队理解这个愿景，因为我基本上是在说，“登上这艘船，我们将航行到百慕大或某个岛屿的愿景”，然后我描述这个美丽的岛屿。他们必须被说服并坚信他们想要到达那里并一起乘船航行。 (00:44:20)：所以团队是最大的部分，是整个团队。这不仅仅是产品经理的愿景。我们只是设计师，就是愿景。我将首先从房间里的每个人开始。我们基本上会将我们的团队聚集在一起并展示一个应用程序。例如，我们去年所做的，我们向我们所谓的工作室领导展示了它，这本质上是每个产品团队的三元组、PM、工程和每个产品团队的设计，然后就把它展示了出来。我有多个。 (00:44:50)：我们有第一个。然后我每周都会在我的产品经理中提出一个问题，然后再次提出，“嘿伙计们，还有什么问题吗？”因为人们仍然……它正在渗透。就像茶包一样。它正在渗出。他们试图理解它并尝试对其进行压力测试。我还做的就是写下研讨会的成果。所以我总是会写输出。这些是我们得出的见解。这是基于时间框架的内容。这是策略。这里有大石头，一个异象正在来临。 (00:45:18)：然后我们会做异象并说：“但是，如果我们做所有这些事情，这就是我们要去的地方。”这将是一个动态文档，评论，开放评论，不能编辑，不能仅查看，评论是因为你希望任何人都可以在那里留下评论，并且感觉他们有发言权。您不必对所有这些问题做出回应。你不必解决所有问题，但只要你把石头放进洗衣机，它们就会互相抛光。我喜欢这种摩擦。 (00:45:47)：我总是喜欢，我走进森林，砍下一块木头，然后我们一起将它打磨成漂亮的丹麦家具。因此，暂时这样做是可以的。然后，一旦团队到达某个地方，我不会试图让任何人获得百分百的确定性，我只是想让你上路。他们会来的，对吗？ (00:46:05)：然后我会进入下一层，即利益相关者，那些进来的人和他们的团队以及他们的经理会去找他们，让他们也参与到愿景中。他们也会带来观点，对吧？你错过了这个作品。我们有很多工程。如果你这样做，支持票就会爆炸。那看起来像什么？你们还没有解决我们今天要做的事情。你说的是五年后的事情。 (00:46:32)：您将获得各种不同的反馈。没关系。人们已经相信了这个故事的核心。拥有所有这些都是可以的……最后，一旦你得到了利益相关者的反馈，你就可以去找领导层，而且领导层确实尽可能高。所以当我在 Uber 工作时，我就像一个 L-5、L-6，我一直有愿景。我的意思是我有一位出色的领导者。他让我全体上台来展示这个愿景。我们就像一个钱包，拥有所有 Uber 体验。然后我们就有这样的愿景：一个 Uber Eats 优食的世界，它可以是火车，也可以是任何东西，你拥有一个可以用于所有这些的 Uber 钱包。我们对它的样子进行了嘲笑。 (00:47:13)：所以尽可能大。做大。让人们告诉你撤退。让你的经理使用套索把你拉回来。尽可能去。所以我去找领导层，然后我有了领导层，我必须尽可能多地找到那个故事。这就是三个同心圆。核心团队，实际构建这个东西的人，利益相关者，需要让这个东西成功的人，因为他们发挥了作用，以及相邻团队，因为当我们构建这个东西时，这可能意味着我们对你的某个请求或某件事说不，最后是领导力。这很难。
